opus-5.5.text:
I think it really comes down to a few things, and the first one, honestly, is how much the embodiments share at the level of the task rather than at the level of the hardware.

When people first started thinking about cross-embodiment learning, the intuition was that it would only work if the robots looked alike: same number of joints, similar kinematics, similar grippers. And of course that helps. If you have two seven-degree-of-freedom arms with parallel-jaw grippers, the low-level motor skills transfer pretty naturally. But what we've seen, and this was one of the more surprising lessons from pooling data across many different robots, is that a lot of the transfer actually happens at a higher level. Things like understanding what "pick up the cup" means visually, where the cup is, what a good grasp looks like, what the scene should look like when the task succeeds. That kind of knowledge is largely embodiment-agnostic, and a model trained on data from many different robots gets better at it because it simply sees more of the world.

So the second factor is the action representation. If every robot speaks a completely different "language" of actions, say joint torques for one, joint positions for another, end-effector velocities for a third, then the model has to learn a separate mapping for each, and the shared knowledge gets bottlenecked. If you can find a common action space, for example end-effector poses in a consistent frame, or even something more abstract, then you open up a much bigger channel for transfer. A lot of the engineering work is really about choosing that shared interface well.

Third is the diversity and balance of the data. If one embodiment dominates the dataset, the model tends to overfit to its quirks, and the others become second-class citizens. What you want is enough variety that the model is forced to learn what's common and treat the embodiment-specific parts as just conditioning information. In a sense, diversity is what makes the abstraction emerge.

And then the fourth thing is model capacity. With small models, adding data from a different robot can actually hurt, because there's negative interference: the model doesn't have room to represent both. As models get larger, that interference goes down and you start to see positive transfer. That's very similar to what happened in language models with multilingual training. Small models got worse when you added more languages; big models got better at all of them.

So if I had to summarize: transfer is effective when the tasks share semantics, when you have a good common action representation, when the data is diverse and balanced, and when the model is big enough to absorb the differences. Where it still breaks down is at the very physical level, such as contact-rich manipulation, dynamics, and very different morphologies like going from an arm to a legged robot. That's where I think a lot of the interesting open problems are right now.

r001.rationale: It says transfer still breaks down at the physical level, including when moving between very different morphologies such as an arm and a legged robot.

r002.rationale: It discusses data diversity and imbalance, but does not say that abundant data for the target robot reduces the added benefit of transfer.

r003.rationale: It describes benefits from pooling data across robots, but does not state that transfer is especially effective from a data-rich embodiment to a target embodiment with hard-to-collect data.

fable-5.1.text:
Jie Tan: That's a question I've thought about a lot, because transfer across embodiments is really the thing that decides whether robot learning scales or stays a one-robot-at-a-time craft.

I'd say there are three big factors. The first is how much the embodiments actually share in the structure of the problem. If two robots have roughly similar morphology and similar action spaces, say two different quadrupeds, or two arms with grippers, transfer is relatively easy. The policy only has to adapt the details. But when you go from a quadruped to a humanoid, or from an arm to a mobile manipulator, the mapping from what the robot sees to what it should do changes fundamentally, and a lot of what the model learned stops being useful.

The second factor is the representation. If you train on raw joint positions and torques, the policy is tightly bound to that one body. If you lift the representation to something more abstract, like end-effector poses, contact events, or the task-level intent, then a lot more carries over. In a sense the question is what layer of the stack you ask the learning to happen at. The higher and more semantic the layer, the more transferable, but the more you depend on a good low-level controller underneath.

The third factor, and I think the most underrated, is the diversity of the training data. When we trained on a single robot, the model implicitly memorized that robot. When we trained across many robots, even imperfectly, the model started to learn which parts of behavior are about the task and which parts are about the body. That separation is what makes transfer possible. So the recipe is not so different from what happened in language and vision: diversity and scale force the model to find the invariants.

And then there's a practical point. Transfer is never zero-shot in the real world. There's always some calibration, some fine-tuning on the new embodiment. The real metric is how much data you need on the new robot to get to good performance. If that goes from months to a few hours, that's a successful transfer, even if it isn't literally free.

r001.rationale: The response says transfer is relatively easy for robots with similar morphology, while moving between substantially different embodiments makes the mapping change fundamentally and learning less useful.

r002.rationale: It discusses training data diversity and how much new-robot data transfer requires, but does not say that abundant data for the target robot reduces transfer’s incremental benefit.

r003.rationale: It says training across many robots can support transfer, but does not specifically describe transfer from a data-rich embodiment to a target embodiment where data is difficult to collect.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends on how much structure the two embodiments share, and at what level you’re trying to transfer knowledge. For example, deciding which object to pick up can be quite similar across robots. But the joint motions and forces needed to pick it up can be very different if you change the gripper or the arm.

So the representation matters a lot. Can we learn something about the task and the environment that is shared, while allowing each robot to learn how to execute it with its own body? Differences in sensing, action space, and dynamics all affect how difficult that separation is.

And then there’s the diversity of the training experience. If you train on only one robot, the policy can become very specialized to that robot. Training across different embodiments gives it an opportunity to learn what’s common. The practical test is whether that shared knowledge lets a new robot learn with less data and less interaction than it would need starting from scratch.

r001.rationale: The response says transfer depends on how much structure the embodiments share and that changing the gripper or arm can make execution very different, linking embodiment differences to transfer difficulty.

r002.rationale: It does not say that abundant data for the target robot reduces the added benefit of transfer.

r003.rationale: It says training across embodiments may help a new robot use less data, but does not specify abundant data for the source embodiment or difficulty collecting data for the target.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot depends on what is shared between the embodiments and what level you’re trying to transfer. If two robots have similar bodies, actuators, and sensors, you may be able to transfer fairly low-level control skills. If their bodies are very different, it makes more sense to transfer higher-level knowledge—what the task requires, how to break it into steps—and let each robot learn how to execute those steps with its own body.

The representation is really important. Can you describe a skill in terms of the effect you want in the world, rather than a particular robot’s joint commands? “Move this object to that location” is much more transferable than a sequence of motor torques.

And then there’s adaptation. The transferred knowledge gives you a starting point, but the robot still needs experience to account for its own dynamics and limitations. So I would judge transfer by how much it reduces the data and interaction needed to learn on the new robot, rather than expecting the same policy to work unchanged everywhere.

r001.rationale: It says that when robot bodies are very different, low-level transfer is less suitable and higher-level knowledge should be transferred instead, conveying that greater morphological differences make transfer more difficult.

r002.rationale: The response discusses reducing the data and interaction needed on the new robot, but does not say that abundant target-robot training data reduces transfer’s incremental benefit.

r003.rationale: It does not compare source and target data availability or say that transfer is especially effective when the source has abundant data and target data is difficult to collect.
